These two caliphs introduced important reforms in the organization of the state. They created a currency of its own, standardized systems of government administration, surveyed and registered land in Arabic, and replaced the older local languages with Arabic throughout the state’s administration and official offices.
The class character of the Umayyad state appeared in several other ways as well, apart from the general semi-feudal character of its social system.
The Umayyad government, and especially Muʿāwiya’s government, allowed the existing local ruling class to keep many of its old powers, including authority over courts and policing.
Later, when state institutions were Arabized under the Marwanid caliphs, these powers passed instead to groups close to the ruling class.
The form had changed, but the class character remained. Given the class character of the state itself, this was only to be expected.
During the early years of their rule, the Umayyads tried to offer some new advantages to the original inhabitants of the conquered regions.
In Iran, for example, they reduced some of the enormous inequalities in rights and duties that had existed under the old social order between the upper and lower classes.
They also reduced taxes on Nabataeans and Syriacs in Egypt and Syria, and they did not force them to convert to Islam.
But during the final decades of Umayyad rule, a combination of objective conditions and choices made by the rulers themselves changed this policy.
Harsh and arbitrary treatment of the lower social groups became increasingly common, both in setting taxes and in collecting them.

The Umayyads also changed an earlier rule introduced at the beginning of the conquests. At first, people who converted to Islam had been exempted from the jizya, while the kharāj, or land tax, was collected from those who owned or worked the land.
Later, people in this position were sometimes made to pay both taxes: the jizya and the kharāj.
This helped provoke repeated uprisings against Umayyad rule in several regions.

One example came in Central Asia in the year 73 AH (728 CE), followed by further revolts in the years that followed. These uprisings came close not only to destroying Umayyad rule in the region, but to ending the Arab presence there altogether.
Another important change under the Umayyads concerned land ownership among the conquering Arabs.

At the beginning of the conquests, under the Rightly Guided Caliphs and especially under ʿUmar, the Arabs had lived largely apart from the original inhabitants. They remained in the military cities that had originally been built for the armies.
Their children therefore took little part in production, and ʿUmar strictly prevented the Arabs from owning land in the conquered territories.
All of this changed under the Umayyads.
Arab communities that had arrived with the conquering armies were now allowed to acquire as much land as they wished in these regions.

Naturally, only some members of these communities could actually do so. They were, first, those wealthy enough to buy and develop land and, second, those with family or political connections to the Umayyad government.

The major Arabic historical sources—including the works of al-Ṭabarī, al-Balādhurī, and al-Yaʿqūbī—show that the estates acquired by Umayyad families and their supporters became so large and productive that enormous wealth became concentrated in the hands of a small new Arab class.
The same sources also show that by the late Umayyad period, conditions for the people working these large estates had become extremely harsh.

These workers included local peasants and enslaved captives. Their living conditions became so poor, and epidemic disease so destructive, that the system itself began to hold back further development of production.
This helped weaken the Umayyad state in its final years.

It faced repeated uprisings, first from groups whose anger came directly from social conditions; second from the political and factional opponents of the Umayyads; and third from non-Arab groups who remained deeply hostile to the Umayyads because of their policy of discrimination between Arabs and the mawālī.

Before ending our discussion of the social system under Umayyad rule, a fair and objective account requires us to recognize other achievements of Muʿāwiya that contributed to development and relative progress.
One was his concern with developing both agriculture and industry in Syria throughout his rule there.
In agriculture, he worked to improve irrigation and increase the fertility of the land. As we have already seen, he made use of specialists from the local population.

In industry, he strengthened customs protections for locally produced goods. This helped local industries develop further, increased their contribution to public revenue and trade, and improved both the skills and the living standards of craftsmen.
Another historically important development began while Muʿāwiya was governor of Syria, during the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
With Muʿāwiya himself taking a special interest in the project, the Arabs began building their first naval fleet.
Here again they made use of local specialists. They also used Lebanese cedar, just as the ancient Phoenicians had done.
The fleet was first used during the Arab conquest of Cyprus.

Later, under Muʿāwiya himself, it was used twice in campaigns against Constantinople. The first took place in 668 and ended in failure. The second began in 673 and succeeded in defeating the Greek fleet and entering the Bosporus and the Golden Horn. Constantinople was then besieged for around five years.
But all these reforms were also required by the way the productive forces were developing—first and foremost in agriculture, and then in craft production as its techniques became more advanced.
The social system represented by the Umayyad state was, through its own development, moving toward greater trade and toward more skilled forms of craft production.
The system itself was opening up new possibilities. Agriculture and irrigation, in particular, increasingly required more advanced tools.

At the same time, the ruling class, large landowners, wealthy merchants, and military commanders had growing resources of their own. They could afford expensive and technically advanced goods for consumption and private ownership.
And because the state was constantly expanding, weapons production also had to develop to meet its military needs.

We have now looked at several features of the economic, social, and political conditions that accompanied Umayyad rule, from its foundation under Muʿāwiya to the period when the state began weakening under the combined pressures that eventually brought it down.
But for the purposes of our present study, we now need to identify some of the historical events that took the form of uprisings, rebellions, or organized opposition to Umayyad rule.
These events produced important effects in the world of ideas.

By the late seventh and early eighth centuries, they brought developing Arab thought directly face to face with social and political reality. They created a connection between thought and reality that could not be hidden even by the relative independence that thought can acquire when it becomes capable of dealing with abstract theoretical problems, or when artistic creation seems to rise far above the immediate world of everyday life.
These historical events followed one another rapidly and often overlapped in ways that were both striking and complex.
For now, we need to select the events most clearly connected with our subject, especially those involving the Shiʿa and the Kharijites, to whom this chapter is devoted.
We will not enter here into the familiar debate over when the term Shiʿa first appeared historically or as the name of a religious group.

Did it begin during the lifetime of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib? After the martyrdom of his son al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī at Karbala? Or even earlier, during the lifetime of the Prophet, as some modern writers on the subject argue?
In this study, by Shiʿa we mean those Muslims to whom the term later came to be applied without dispute because they supported—literally, took the side of—ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.

They regarded him as the person with the legitimate, divinely sanctioned right to succeed the Prophet immediately as caliph, followed in turn by his direct descendants according to the recognized line of succession.

The Shiʿa in this sense launched several uprisings during the political, religious, and ideological struggles that followed the end of the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and continued throughout Umayyad rule.
Here, however, we are concerned specifically with the first Shiʿi uprising against Umayyad power.

After ʿAlī was killed in Kufa by one of the Khārijites, while Muʿāwiya escaped the attempt on his own life by another Khārijite, Muʿāwiya hoped to secure the caliphate for himself through political maneuvering rather than war. He achieved this when he reached an agreement with al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, who, according to Shiʿi belief, should have become caliph after his father.

Under the agreement, al-Ḥasan gave up his claim to the caliphate in favor of Muʿāwiya, on the condition that the caliphate would pass to him after Muʿāwiya’s death. Muʿāwiya accepted this condition, but he already had another plan in mind and had begun preparing for it. He wanted to establish a hereditary Umayyad state, with the throne passing after him from one of his descendants to the next.

At the same time, he wanted to avoid any upheaval that might threaten his own rule. So he reluctantly accepted al-Ḥasan’s condition. “But Muʿāwiya could not rest easy while al-Ḥasan was alive and his pledge to him still stood.” Perhaps he had already decided that he would somehow free himself from this obligation so that nothing would stand in the way of his plan. Shiʿis believe that Muʿāwiya did in fact free himself from it by having al-Ḥasan poisoned in 49 AH/669 CE.

Whatever the truth of that claim, the death of the second Shiʿi imam left Muʿāwiya much more confident about the future of his plan. He was now free of his pledge to al-Ḥasan. The only remaining obstacle to naming his son Yazīd as heir to the throne was the reaction he expected from the leading Companions of the Prophet who were still alive, and from much of Arab-Islamic public opinion.

The idea itself was new and strange in Islam. And in the eyes of many Muslims, Yazīd was not fit for the position. But Muʿāwiya had such firm control over affairs that he was willing to go ahead despite the opposition he knew he might face.

Muʿāwiya was bold enough in confronting Arab-Islamic public opinion that he even had a number of prominent Companions of the Prophet killed, among them Ḥujr ibn ʿAdī and his companions. He showed no hesitation about this. In fact, during one meeting with al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, he boasted about it in a mood of triumph and spite.

With the same boldness, he named his son Yazīd as heir. Yazīd thus became the first designated heir to the caliphate in Islamic history. From that point on, hereditary succession became a normal practice under the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs, and under later dynasties as well, apart from a few periods, down to the Ottoman revolution in Constantinople—Istanbul—at the beginning of the twentieth century, in 1908.
Muʿāwiya died in 680 CE, and Yazīd took the throne because his father had already made him heir.

Many people opposed this. The first open resistance to Yazīd’s caliphate came from the Shiʿa of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in Kufa. They had learned that their third imam, al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, who was then in Mecca, had refused to pledge allegiance to Yazīd as caliph. They sent delegations to al-Ḥusayn, inviting him to come to Kufa and lead their uprising against Yazīd and against the Umayyad caliphate itself.

Al-Ḥusayn accepted their invitation and decided to leave Mecca for Kufa. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, one of the leading Companions of the Prophet and a cousin of al-Ḥusayn’s father ʿAlī, advised him not to go. Ibn ʿAbbās told him:
“Go to Yemen. It is remote, and you have supporters and brothers there. Stay there and send out your callers.”
But al-Ḥusayn believed that he had a duty to resist Yazīd and the Umayyad throne, especially now that he seemed to have the people he needed in Kufa.

When al-Ḥusayn reached Iraq on his way to Kufa, he learned that many of the supporters who had invited him to rise up and had promised to fight under his banner had lost their nerve. The governor of Kufa, ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād, who supported the Umayyads, had used threats and intimidation against some of them, and promises and bribes against others.

Al-Ḥusayn was now in a very difficult position. He could return to the Hijaz and risk being accused of weakness and of abandoning something he believed to be his duty. Or he could continue toward a battle with Yazīd’s army, even though he had brought women and children with him and now had only a very small number of supporters left.
He chose to go forward rather than turn back.

He continued until he met the Umayyad army at Karbala. The battle that followed became one of the most distinctive and powerful events of the period. It ended with the killing of al-Ḥusayn, his supporters, and some of his sons, while the women and children of his family were taken prisoner. This happened in 61 AH/680 CE.

At first glance, this first uprising against the first hereditary Umayyad caliph might seem, especially when told in such simple terms, like an ordinary event with little place in a discussion of historical movements that shaped the development of thought.
But that would badly distort the historical reality.

The uprising cannot be understood simply as the short battle at Karbala and its immediate result: the overwhelming victory that the Umayyad army won within a few hours over the small group of al-Ḥusayn’s supporters—some 300 fighters.

What defines this Shiʿi uprising historically is what happened after the battle of the tenth of Muḥarram in 61 AH, when its leader, the third Shiʿi imam, was killed. Its importance also comes from the political and intellectual effects that continued to spread, both deeply and widely, throughout the period we are discussing.

The lasting force of this uprising does not come simply from its tragic character. A modern view, no longer caught up in the intense emotions of the event itself, must look beyond the tragedy and reach the less dramatic forces underneath it.
Seen in that way, the following factors become clear.

We need to look closely at Muʿāwiya’s decision to change the caliphate from the consultative system associated with the Rightly Guided caliphs into a hereditary form of personal rule that was close to monarchy.
This was not a small change that could simply be imposed without expecting serious opposition from large parts of Muslim public opinion.

Muʿāwiya managed to carry it out during his lifetime by combining force with political maneuvering. But the fact that he avoided a major storm while he was alive does not mean that no storm was forming beneath the surface of Arab-Islamic society, waiting for something to bring it out into the open.

Large numbers of Arabs and Muslims, including leading Companions of the Prophet and the generation that followed them, did not find it easy to accept what Muʿāwiya had done, even if outward appearances sometimes suggested otherwise.

We can even say that generations of Muslim religious scholars, historians, and researchers continued, down to the modern period, to look on Muʿāwiya’s action with disapproval, or at least with genuine unease.

Al-Maqrīzī relates that one Muslim jurist, who lived much later than the Umayyad period, was once asked why Muslim kings so often failed to follow the right path and paid no respect to “covenant or sanctity.” He replied:

“That is because kingship has no place in our religious law. Our law recognizes only caliphs. Abū Bakr was the caliph of the Messenger of God, even though the Prophet had not expressly appointed him in a text. But people understood the matter that way and unanimously called him caliph.

“Then Abū Bakr appointed ʿUmar. In doing so, he took the office away from the path of kingship, in which a son inherits from his father, and placed it on the path of the caliphate, which rests on judgment and choice. He stated this clearly in his appointment.
“Then the people of the council agreed on ʿUthmān. The fact that ʿUmar moved the office away from the structure of kingship and placed it under consultation proves that it was not kingship.
“Then ʿAlī became the obvious choice, since no one like him remained. Those who preferred truth to desire and the next world to this one pledged allegiance to him. Then came al-Ḥasan in the same way.

“Muʿāwiya was the first to turn the caliphate into kingship, and austerity into ease. And after that, your Lord is indeed forgiving and merciful. He made the caliphate hereditary. Once he took it away from its proper form, no kingship remained upright.
“Do you not see that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—may God be pleased with him—was a caliph, not a king? No one ever followed the straight path except a caliph.”
These words come from a jurist who lived long after the Umayyads, yet they show how deeply Muʿāwiya’s action continued to trouble Muslims across the generations.
The bitterness in his words is obvious. Even after so much time had passed, he still spoke with deep resentment about Muʿāwiya’s decision to turn the caliphate into hereditary monarchy.
If people felt this way generations later, what must Muslims have felt during Muʿāwiya’s own lifetime?
